The Raps can only wish it were as easy as this stat makes it sound: Toronto is 8-0 when its much-maligned defence (Canadian spelling) finds a way to hold the opposition below 100 points … and 3-15 otherwise.

At least one thing is going according to plan for the Raps: Bosh has racked up a league-leading 13 games with at least 25 points and 10 boards. That's six more than his closest pursuer: New Jersey's Brook Lopez.

There was no guarantee, knowing how these Raps play D, that they could capitalize on what looked to be a favorable stretch of schedule. But they'll finish 5-0 in this targeted stretch if they beat Charlotte on Wednesday.

The Raps showed us something by beating the Spurs. No Hedo/Calderon and still they proved momentum from the 5-0 stretch wasn't lost when they failed to steal one in Boston with Pierce, KG and Rondo all out.

Jim from Chicago wrote in to ask why we haven't been trotting out our trusty Leastern Conference references. And he certainly has a point when the Raps needed an 8-2 surge just to give the East six .500 teams.

It took a 10-3 surge, lots of Bosh damage and Jarrett Jack's emergence as the starting point guard to get there, but the Raps are a winning team at the 41-game mark for just the fifth time in the franchise's 15 seasons.

Catch that quote from Canada's foremost free agent-to-be? "I haven't been this encouraged in a while," Bosh says. And that was before Hedo's clutch drive and FTs pulled out that one-point win Sunday over the Lakers.

For a group frequently tagged as soft, this is momentous: Toronto just became the first team since November 2002 to trail by at least 10 points in four straight games and win all four. Foes: Knicks, Heat, Lakers and Bucks.

Since that 146-115 humbling in Atlanta on Dec. 2 and the team meeting that followed, Toronto is 21-10. Which almost -- almost -- atones for the 130 points allowed to Indy after we moved the Raps all the way to No. 7.

The good news? Toronto played at home on nine straight Sundays heading into the All-Star break and quietly went 8-1 in those games. The bad news? The Raptors have only two Sunday home games left all season.

The Raps are 20-7 since their 11-17 start. They made it through the trade deadline having endured only minimal Bosh speculation. And they know Colangelo is staying as GM whether Bosh stays or not. Pretty good times.

The Bulls and Bucks are surging while Bosh -- openly dreaming of a top-four slot during All-Star Weekend -- can't shake his sprained ankle. Add it all up and the East's bottom four playoff seeds are suddenly up for grabs.

The post-Olympics euphoria is going to wear off eventually. Good thing, then, that Bosh is finally back after a seven-game absence that saw the Raps lose all their mojo under the cover of Canada winning hockey gold.

No wonder Bosh went off on his teammates for "not fighting at all." The Raps are 0-5 since his return from injury, including a 13-point home L to Philly and road Ls to the Kings and Warriors by a combined (gulp) 35 points.

You get a full pardon if you're struggling to muster much enthusiasm for the "race" for No. 8 in the East when the teams currently sitting eighth and ninth -- Toronto and Chicago -- are a combined 4-16 in March.

Astonishing how fragile this team is. Losing its way when Bosh went down right after the All-Star Game was understandable, but he's been back for 12 games. The Raps' decline has reached 3-9 and might not be over.

If you had an inkling that the Raptors' playoff credentials were a bit suspect -- and Sunday's home loss to Golden State didn't confirm those suspicions -- this should do it: Toronto is 12-31 against teams .500 or better.

The combo of five straight L's and Bosh's busted nose -- if it has finally KO'd these guys -- sends Bosh to free agency with a Raps sheet featuring two trips to the playoffs and one winning record in seven seasons.

hou.summary: That they've won twice already shouldn't surprise you. You knew going in about the gutty little Rockets, no matter who's in the lineup. The shocker, if you're looking for one, is Ariza averaging 29.0 ppg in those wins.

Still trying to pinpoint exactly what this team's ceiling is without Yao and T-Mac, but it already seems safe to say that the gutty little Rockets will spend all season right at the top of the list of teams no one wants to play.

You watch the Rockets win on the Lakers' floor and you hear that they've scored 100 points or more in nine straight games for the first time since 1995-96 and you understand why there's hesitation to rush T-Mac back.
The forthcoming docket for the gutty little Rockets: Dallas at home Wednesday, San Antonio at home Friday and then a trip to Oklahoma City on Sunday. A week doesn't get more Southwestern-y than that.

GM Daryl Morey, via Twitter, on the new Rockets: "We cannot win if we are in [a half-court game] as much as [the] opponent." As for the tweeted conclusion you did expect from him: "We have little margin for error."

Lil' Aaron Brooks is generally seen as the offensive face of this scrappy incarnation of the Rockets. Just don't forget Carl Landry and his nine 20-point games ... after just four of those in his previous two seasons.

If Ariza gets suspended, as expected, for his tangle with Toronto, we'll have to scratch Houston's undersized Cinderellas from the list of teams to use the same starting five in every game. Boston is the only other team.

Only one team out West (Phoenix) has played more roadies than the Rockets. And Houston gets to make an extra trip to Dallas if the league upholds the Mavs' protest because it already made its two trips to Big D.

Spokesman Battier sizing up the West's best Cinderellas to the NY Times: "We have a collection of guys who [were] told they're too 'something' to play in the NBA. Too small, too short, too dumb, can't shoot, unathletic."

If Westphal isn't your COY so far, it's got to be Adelman. He's moved into Sloan territory as one of the best never to win the COY thanks to what these no-name Rockets are doing with the hardest schedule to date.

These Rockets have been so good at ignoring injury obstacles that you naturally expect them to grind through the trade rumors, too. Knowing that an easier second-half schedule is forthcoming should help the mood.

I know that T-Mac gets lots of All-Star votes in China. I still say that T-Mac holding off Nash and CP3 to snag a starting guard spot in the West would be as surprising as anything we've seen from the Rockets all season.

The Rockets have slumped to 4-6 in January. So you're starting to see why they'd part with T-Mac's monster expiring contract before the deadline if they could net a surefire star. You can win with scrappiness for only so long.

More evidence that relying so much on scrappiness is gradually taking its toll: Houston is 1-4 on this six-game homestand to fall to 14-9 at the Toyota Center. Last season? The Rockets lost eight home games total.

How hard to beat have the Rockets been in their own building? Saturday night's unexpected L to Philly -- wasting Aaron Brooks' sixth 30-point game of the season -- was their first February loss at home since Feb. 28, 2007.

Almost missed this one with all of the attention hoarded by the T-Mac trade talks: Houston's recent nightmare trip to Miami marked the only time this season that a team with a winning record failed to score 70 points.

It's going to be tough for the Rockets, geeked as they are about the trade for Kevin Martin, to look back fondly on February. They're 1-5 in their past six games and tied for 10th in the West after a 3-5 mark this month.

Good news: Houston was the first team in 15 years with three 30-point scorers (Martin, Brooks and Scola) in a non-OT game. Bad news: The W they netted over the Parker-less Spurs is Houston's only W post-trade.

All Scola has to do is keep this up -- 21.3 points and 18.0 boards over his past three games -- and Houstonians will (eventually) get over the fact that their Rockets had to surrender Landry in the Kevin Martin deal.

We were half-joking when we suggested Scola's hot streak could make Houstonians forget about Landry, but maybe the snark got lost in translation. Scola's up to 26.2 ppg and 15.2 rpg in his past five games.

The Rockets have won five out of six and have played three fewer games than the Blazers, whom they trail by 4 1/2 games. Maybe all that means there's still hope for a decent race for the West's final playoff spot.

Nope. We were obviously reaching last week when we dared to suggest that the Rockets still had some playoff life. They're 1-5 since the four-game win streak that sucked us in, which shifts all of our focus back onto Scola.

It's a successful season even without a playoff berth for the injury-ravaged Rockets. Quite the style transformation, too. This is how vital running is to them now: Houston is 0-16 when it scores less than 95 points.

There's too much traffic in the COY race for Adelman to score many votes, but the campaign for Best Team Ever Without An All-Star is still worth waging according to Adelman's boss, who expounds on that claim here.

nop.summary: Two games is way too soon to talk about coaching changes. Even in the hyper-speculative NBA. But I still wouldn't have wanted to be Byron Scott if the Hornets didn't pull out that home opener against the Kings' kiddies.

The first 8-0 start in Saints history -- someone had to tell us because you know we wouldn't have known otherwise -- theoretically takes some pressure off these guys. Or maybe it's one more thing that steams CP3.

Byron Scott gets the rest of this season's $5 million salary no matter what. Jeff Bower loses Chris Paul in his debut as an NBA head coach ... and the Hornets have holes aplenty with CP3. Who would you rather be?

Byron Scott, truth be told, began the season with little chance of survival. But his reluctance to play Collison and Thornton -- rookies who, with Peja, just sparked wins over Phoenix and Atlanta -- sealed B-Scott's fate.

Whatever weird mojo makes the Hornets unbeatable at home as long as the game goes to OT -- they've won 11 straight OT games at their place -- worked against Milwaukee even with CP3 out. So something's working.

The Hornets are 5-5 under Jeff Bower because they somehow went 4-4 after CP3 hurt his ankle in Bower's opening game. We frankly expected none of that ... especially those home wins over Phoenix and Atlanta.

After gamely splitting those eight games without Chris Paul, New Orleans was heading for a 4-0 mark since CP3's return ? until the Hornets surrendered the final, yes, 18 points at home Friday night to the Knicks.

Even though he just missed on a triple-double, CP3's 30 points, 19 assists and nine boards against Denver make for a historic line. No one has hit those levels in the same game since Magic Johnson and Fat Lever in 1988.

If the Hornets hadn't managed to play .500 ball for an eight-game stretch without CP3 -- pretty much the worst adversity they could face -- it'd be easier to accept that they have the NBA's third-worst road record at 2-12.

The Hornets' season could hinge on this month. They're as active as anyone on the trade front and have ample opportunity to spruce up that 2-13 road record with 11 of the next 15 games away from home.
See what happens when we throw some committee (of one) spotlight on the Hornets' 2-13 road record? They win three roadies in the span of a week. Who would dare say these rankings don't mean anything?

The Hornets are 18-12 since Byron Scott's dismissal and had to play without an injured CP3 for eight of those 30 games. It doesn't hurt that D-West and Okafor are starting to look like a workable frontcourt tag team.

Even we know enough about American football to know that the Saints getting to the Super Bowl is a historic deal. But don't blame us if the focus here is on whether the Hornets will find it inspiring. Or pressure-raising.

The Hornets had won 11 straight overtime games at home, dating all the way to March 2005 when they were playing in OKC, before Friday's disastrous OT loss to Chicago, during which they lost the streak and CP3.

It's quite possible that the long-suffering sports fans of New Orleans haven't even realized yet that CP3 just had knee surgery. And after what the Saints just did? He might even make it back before anyone really notices.

Hanging in there without CP3 is proving tougher for the Hornets this time, even though they couldn't ask more of rookie fill-in Collison. They're 2-4 since losing Paul to a knee problem after going 4-4 during his first absence.

The best rookie no one talks much about? Collison is a huge reason the Hornets are 9-9 this season when CP3 is out. They're 4-2 in their past six games, with DC scoring at least 24 points five times in that span.

Thanks to his 35-point signoff in Dallas, Collison averaged 21.6 points and 8.3 assists for the month. Only one other rook in the past 25 years can top those totals: Allen Iverson (33.6 points and 8.7 assists) in April 1997.

This is already Chris Paul's most painful season yet in terms of games lost to injury, easily topping the 18 games he lost -- mostly to a bad ankle -- in the 2006-07 season. The '09-10 Hornets are 10-15 without him.

It's probably time to press pause on all the recent fawning over Collison and Thornton, no matter how good they've been lately, since almost every other Hornet you've ever heard of is hurt, resulting in a 1-7 skid.

The Hornets managed to split their first 18 games this season without CP3, but expecting that kind of success to last for half a season was unrealistic. This inevitable 3-12 spiral dropped N.O. to 12-21 when he's in street clothes.

We get that no one in the organization wanted to tell the ultracompetitive CP3 that it's better for the franchise (and his own good) to just sit out the rest of the regular season. Doesn't stop us from fearing the worst, though.

The Hornets have dropped 11 of 14, they've lost five of seven since Chris Paul's comeback and the playoffs are long gone. So we beg of thee, CP3: Shut it down for the rest of the season. Playing any more is a needless risk.

We'd like to think our pleas in this cyberspace last week to convince CP3 to shut it down for the rest of the season played at least some small part in that decision. So, yes, we're still quite delusional after all these years.

okc.summary: We repeat: Give 'em time. A 2-0 launch was nice, especially when it includes a 1-0 road record, but Sunday's home test against Portland was an early reminder that the NW Division's young darlings are still evolving.

It's just Stan Van Gundy venting after a loss without Rashard and Vince, but I imagine OKC folks will enjoy reading it: "The Thunder are much better than us right now. They would have [won] if we had everybody."

OKC's defense/length/athleticism seen in San Antonio suggest this team can handle seven roadies in nine games just fine . . . except that it bookended that win with an L in Sacramento and a home L to the Clips.

Sunday's lesson from the Lakers dropped OKC's record to 10-43 in its past 53 games against teams that showed up with a winning record. But you have to believe that mark won't look so one-sided by season's end.

Morey after Houston inflicted Oklahoma City's fourth home loss: "Huge W against vastly improved OKC [team] playing like a top-10 [team]." Top-15 is more like it, but add him to the (growing) list of Thunder admirers.

As if Blazermaniacs weren't suffering enough after Oden's latest setback, this haunting tidbit circulated late Friday: Durant just became the second-youngest player in history to get to 4,000 points, behind only LeBron.

OKC didn't record its 12th victory last season until Feb. 6. The Thunder, though, have too many road games and too many good teams left on their December schedule to spend much time basking in their progress.

The shocker is not that the Thunder are a 0-5 when their franchise player is held below 20 points. The shocker is that we just saw it happen twice to young Durant in Oklahoma City's most recent three games.

Factoids, factoids, factoids: OKC is 12-1 when it puts up 100 points, Durant has 13 30-point games already and the Thunder reached 15 wins on the day after Christmas ... after needing until March 2 to get there last season.

What excites you most, OKC? Durant's seven straight 30-point games? That your nearly vet-less team inched past .500? Or how many guys it has stolen (Sefolosha, Krstic and Maynor) thanks to financial flexibility?

The word for Durant's past 10 games is ridiculous: 32.7 ppg on 57.4 percent shooting and 47.1 percent on 3s. In related news, OKC has quadrupled its win total from last season's 5-31 mark at the same point.

Found some Durant minutiae Simmons hasn't covered with his fawny tweets: Durant's 14 straight games with at least 25 points is second all time for players before their 22nd birthdays behind LeBron's 16 in a row.

Instead of the usual array of gaudy Durant numbers here, here's what this young team still learning how to win has been through lately: OKC's past four losses (Spurs, Mavs, Griz, Cavs) came by a total of five points.

January was only Durant's best month as a pro. He averaged 32.1 points for the month and signed off with his fourth 40-point game of the season, placing him fourth in the league behind Kobe (7), Melo (5) and LeBron (5).

My bad: OKC was way too low last Monday and has been hurt more than any team by our recent struggles to sort out the weekly jumble in the middle. At 16-8 during Durant's streak of 25-point games, it had to jump.

Wait a sec. The Thunder had the same record as San Antonio at the All-Star break and only one top-flight finisher? Book it: Durant is going to finish in the top 5 in year-end MVP balloting … and maybe in the top 3.

A trade for a vet would have been nice and ''Durantula'' still doesn't work for me as a nickname, but there isn't much else here to protest. Not when OKC is a tidy 20-8 during Durant's streak of consecutive 25-point games.

Let's get Simmons in one last lather about The Streak: Durant's run of 29 straight games with at least 25 points started before Christmas and spanned a tidy 64 days. The bonus: OKC is up to 22-11 when KD scores 30 or more.

Take it as a compliment, young Mr. Durant, that you're being pestered by media gnats about your OKC future all the time now. That annoyance is yet another sign that you've crashed the game's uppermost stratosphere.

One problem with all the justified slobbering over Durant: We've all shortchanged Westbrook. KD's point guard has racked up seven 20/10 games since Feb. 1, tied with LeBron for tops in the league in that span.

OKC has set the bar so high that you didn't know how to react when it finally threw in a stinker in Indy. It was only the fifth L in 23 games for a team whose leading rebounder -- Durant -- averages a whopping 7.5 rpg.

What strikes you as the more realistic OKC playoff preview? Last week's narrow losses at home to the Spurs and Blazers? Or Friday night's pounding of the Lakers? Sorry to say that, for us, it's probably the former.

Imagine how much trouble the OKC kids are going to cause if they ever acquire or develop a front-line center and get some actual, you know, experience. As it is, they're going to win 50 and could still win their division.

The good news: Durant needs 26 ppg in two games to win the scoring title if LeBron doesn't play again. The bad news: OKC's collapse at Golden State lines Durant up for a playoff baptism against Kobe's Lakers.

det.summary: Latest examples of how Twitter has changed the game: Villanueva responds to back-to-back Ls with a plea to fans to "NOT PRESS THE PANIC BUTTON" and a promise that "WE WILL BE MORE THAN ALL RIGHT."

Rip Hamilton hasn't played since opening night. Persistent back trouble just took down Tayshaun Prince. And rookie Jonas Jerebko has been forced to start four games. Given all that, Detroit's hanging in there OK.

The good news: Gordon, Charlie V, Will Bynum and Big Ben have kept the Pistons competitive. The bad news: Trading Prince -- one of the options they have to bring in some size -- is a lot tougher if Tay has a bad back.

You can rationalize Detroit's 0-4 trip out West when you factor in the quality of the opposition and the Pistons' injury woes. Harder to explain or accept is the fact that Will Bynum has been steadier than Rodney Stuckey.

Detroit's best (and sturdiest) player so far has been a 35-year-old named Ben Wallace. Which would make for a heartwarming story if not for all the losses and injuries that piled up on the Pistons in a rough November.

Bigger surprise: Jonas Jerebko starts 17 of his first 18 NBA games? Or Ben Wallace turns back the clock at 35 to flirt with a double-digit rebound average for the first time since his first season in Chicago in 2006-07?

We were tough on him early when Will Bynum was Detroit's most productive guard, so it's only right to highlight Stuckey's turnaround: 25 or more points in four straight games to spark this five-game win streak.

Can't sum up life with the Pistons these days any better than the AP did after Sunday's lesson from the Lakers. "Three of Detroit's best players wore sport coats: Richard Hamilton, Ben Gordon and Tayshaun Prince."

The good news: Rip, Tayshaun and Ben Gordon are all back in uniform. The bad news: Detroit is already dealing with its second seven-game skid of the season after dropping the Rip/Tay/BG comeback game in Toronto.

How far away from Deeee-troit Bas-ket-ballll have these Pistons strayed? The losing streak has reached a stunning nine defeats in a row and they haven't even managed to take a second-half lead in the last six games.

Q: When does a dozen feel like a bigger number than 10 million? A: When Ben Gordon is credited with scoring the NBA's 10 millionth point in a defeat to Philly that stretches Detroit's losing streak to (yikes) 12 games.

I would never, ever dare to overstate the impact of these rankings, but you tell me: Is it a coincidence that the Pistons started to show a pulse again after slipping all the way to the depths of No. 29? I think not.

Don't know that the Pistons have the goods to get Amare, but perhaps they'll take some heart from the mere knowledge that the kind of player they want -- big man who can score -- just became available in Phoenix.

It's likely time to stop asking whether these Pistons can still sneak into the playoffs for a ninth straight season. After closing a six-game homestand with five straight losses, they're bound for the John Wall Sweepstakes.

No one around the league is giving much credence to the idea that the Pistons could be moving to Pittsburgh, as rumored, but the rumor itself highlights the newfound uncertainty for such a historically stable franchise.

Sunday had to be tough viewing for Detroiters once it morphed into a 2003 draft fest. Wade/LeBron/Bosh finished 1-2-3 in MVP voting, Melo led the West in scoring ... and Jerebko was Detroit's lone All-Star Weekend rep.

ESPN Stats & Information just reminded us that the '03-04 Pistons were the last team before the current Cavs to lose three in a row after 13 straight wins. Doesn't help today's Pistons much, but those Pistons did win it all.

In spite of all its issues, Detroit actually made it to the final two games of February with a record of 6-5 ... only to lose in Denver and Golden State and thus clinch a losing record for the ninth consecutive calendar month.

This week's guest taunt, er, tweet comes from the Power Rankings-loving Sports Guy: "Have the Pistons supplanted the Lions as the most depressing team in Detroit? I can't believe that team was intentionally assembled."

How long has it been since the Pistons were lottery-bound? They began the season clutching the league's third longest streak of consecutive playoff appearances at eight, behind only San Antonio (12) and Dallas (nine).

For one week, at least, let's focus on the positive in Motown: Stuckey ringing up 25 points in his first game back -- even in a loss that dropped Detroit to a demoralizing 0-3 vs. Indy this season -- undoubtedly qualifies.

I'd like to think that becoming just the seventh team to lose to the Nets, thereby ensuring that New Jersey can only share Worst Team of All Time status with the '72-73 Sixers, is rock bottom for the Pistons. I'd like to.

The Pistons just fell 30 games under .500 for the first time since 1993-94, but Charlie V. is still trying to keep it positive on Twitter: "These are some tough times in Detroit, but we need to continue to hang in there."

The guess here is that the 39-point eruption from Ben Gordon that ended Miami's nine-game win streak only wound up reminding folks in Motown how little they've seen of the Gordon (and Villanueva) they were expecting.

cha.summary: It took exactly one game for Charlotte to make its own case that signing A.I. would have helped. They've always had trouble scoring, but even the Bobs had never scored fewer than 73 ... until Boston held them to 59.

Considering that the Bobcats scored fewer than 80 points three times in their first four games and given the teams they've lost to -- Boston, Cleveland and Chicago all on the road -- they can live with a .500 start.

Five times in nine games, Charlotte hasn't made it to 80 points. With MJ making a rare courtside appearance Saturday night? The Bobs scored 74. Hopefully their trade gamble on Jack gives us some new material.

Fearless prediction: Stephen Jackson will not be in Charlotte at season's end. The Bobcats still won't score enough or win enough with Jack to persuade them not to re-shop Jack before the Feb. 18 trade deadline.
Did we wake these guys up or what? Since last week's comment in this cyberspace that the Bobs wouldn't score or win enough to resist shopping Stephen Jackson before the trade deadline, they're 4-0.

Twitterdom can be a cruel place. Check out this crack from our pal BergerSphere late in the loss that ended the Nets' 0-18 start: "Larry Brown is going to quit with 30 seconds left and take the Fordham job."

Stephen Jackson has clearly given the Bobs more belief, but it still ain't happening on the road. Charlotte's away misery includes a loss to the 0-18 Nets and an OT crusher in Dallas that left it 0-11 all-time against the Mavs.

The Bobcats treasure the do-everything versatility of G-Wallace. But responding to a quiet game on the boards for Diaw and Chandler with a quote about heart is presumably not something they wanted him to do.

The Bobs' road woes have become so profound that they have to be grateful this season's schedule isn't as unbalanced as last season's, when 26 of their final 41 games -- and six of eight in April -- were roadies.

A breakthrough in Miami, then an absolute stunner in Cleveland. Larry Brown's Bobs just tripled their total of road wins in the span of a weekend and are going to make their first trip to the playoffs if this keeps up.

You know who's nervous right now? The Houston Texans. They'll be the only franchise in North America's four major sports leagues that hasn't yet tasted the playoffs if the Jackson-Wallace partnership keeps clicking.

In our struggles to sort out Nos. 12-19 last week, Charlotte definitely got the scroogie. We're trying to rectify that with this week's wholly deserved promotion, since the Bobs are 7-1 in 2010 with seven quality W's.

Lost both ends of a barometer back-to-back in Atlanta and at home to Orlando. About to start a rough six-game trip out West, too. But I think we can all still see why Cleveland wanted Stephen Jackson so badly.

I repeat: G-Wallace is an undeniable All-Star, but why is nobody is talking about S-Jax? Jack's partnership with Wallace just sparked the Bobs to 12 wins in January alone. Previous team record for one month? Nine.

Worried as he sounds about how much longer MJ is going to stick around with new owners looming, Larry Brown has done such a good job with the Bobs that he's sure to get another gig if he wants one. Rep restored.

With all the uncertainty about MJ's future -- and corresponding uncertainty about Larry's future -- I already had an "unravel" theme in mind for this space. Then the Bobs came back to work and lost to the Nets. At home.

Some good trivia from our Elias pals: Charlotte just became the first team since Philly in 1985 to lose to the team with the worst record (Nets) and then take down the team with the best record (Cavs) in its next game.

The Mavericks have never lost a game to the Bobs. The Bobs are better than ever at home and will get the Mavs on Monday night after Dallas played l-a-t-e at home Sunday. It's your classic something has to give.

Funny old game, huh? Charlotte just took its record against Dallas to 0-12 lifetime ... and 7-2 against the Lakers since February 2006. Cleveland is the only other team with a winning record against L.A. in that span.

The inclination is to say that a W in Orlando without Gerald Wallace officially stamps the Bobcats as playoff material ... but such declarations would be easier if we knew exactly how long Wallace (foot) is going to be out.

The Bobs can only hope that the first week of MJ's ownership was no omen. They lost in Indy, dropped an OT heartbreaker in Atlanta and scored just 71 points in Miami, reminiscent of their offense before Jack arrived.

Instead of the Bobs' usual nightmare schedule in April, this is reasonable: Six of their final 10 games are at home and the four road dates (Chicago, New Orleans, Houston and New Jersey) aren't exactly unwinnable.

As if the longer-term uncertainty surrounding Larry Brown's future wasn't unsettling enough, here's some short-term cause for panic: Bobcats warrior Stephen Jackson is dealing with a bad hammy, ankle, hand and elbow.

Larry Brown is taking his record eighth NBA club to the playoffs, but we're not sure if this helps or hurts karma-wise: The only expansion team since '88 to win its first-ever playoff series was ... the Charlotte-based Hornets.

lac.summary: The gloom generated by Blake Griffin's knee injury has been replaced by plain old gloom after the Clips went scoreless for the final 4:42 of a home L to Dallas ... with Baron on the bench for all but 19 seconds of the fourth.

The streak of note in Clipperland, given the 3-16 combined record of the three teams they swept last week, is Chris Kaman's streak: 20 points or more in six straight games. His previous best was a mere two in a row.

Did the Clips cool any heat under Mike Dunleavy's seat by winning Sunday at OKC? Better question: How has Dunleavy lasted into his seventh season working for Donald Sterling, who used to fire coaches for sport?

The Clips followed up their good win in OKC by dropping winnable games in New Orleans and Memphis. Let's see if they can build on a good home W over Denver ... especially with Eric Gordon coming back from injury.

Has the worst passed for Mike Dunleavy? We would be asking different questions if not for that epic fourth-quarter comeback against the Griz, but the Clips have quietly gone 4-1 starting with that home win over Denver.

The Clips have won five of their past seven ... and no longer have a share of the NBA's worst start ever thanks to the Nets' plummet to 0-18. So life's not too bad, even if they have to wait until January for Blake Griffin.

Is a January comeback for Blake Griffin -- assuming we're actually going to see him next month as promised -- too late to force his way into the ROY discussion? We're asking for your input because we haven't decided yet.

Just three times all season have teams failed to hold a 20-point lead … with the Clips involved every time. They beat Memphis that way Nov. 29 and lost that way Nov. 13 against Toronto and again Friday in New York.

Simmons' dream is doing these rankings, so we let him help with this one for a change: L.A. is 7-1 against Minnesota, Golden State, Indy, Philly and Washington. And 6-16 against everyone else after Baron sunk Boston.

Kaman refuses to let Zach Randolph roll on unchallenged for the unofficial title of West Big Man Most Egregiously Omitted from the All-Star Ballot. He's up to 10 20-point, 10-rebound games after just two last season.

They'll be patient with Blake Griffin's debut and trading Marcus Camby in hopes of driving up Camby's value between now and the trade deadline. Why rush when you're nearly .500 and just beat the Lakers?

The Clips will soon embark on an eight-game road trip -- yes, eight -- that will determine whether they can hang on in the playoff race ... or if there's no use hanging on to Camby with so many teams eager to trade for him.

Whether he gets there or not, Kaman is certainly keeping All-Star company. Only four players are averaging at least 20 points and nine boards ... and the others on that list are Chris Bosh, Tim Duncan and Zach Randolph.

The Clips have two stops left on an eight-game road trip and are 1-5 on the junket after losses at (gulp) New Jersey and Minnesota. So you tell me: Are we down to 11 teams playing for eight playoff berths in the West?

The Clips are eight games under .500 and 7 1/2 games out of the No. 8 spot after losing Kim Hughes' debut. Which tells you why all the focus now is on Camby's future before the trade deadline as opposed to playoff delusions.

Kim Hughes is still waiting for that honeymoon. The Clips are 0-4 since Hughes replaced Dunleavy, losing by 17 and 10 at home (to San Antonio and Utah) and by 30 and 22 on the road (Golden State and Portland).

After two trades ensured substantial cap space for the summer, Kaman talked up the core he forms with Gordon, Baron and Blake Griffin, then said what we're all thinking: "Do [free agents] want to come to the Clippers?"

Guest comment courtesy of/swiped from the Twitter feed of Arash Markazi at ESPNLosAngeles.com: "What were the odds of the Clippers going 3-0 and the Cavs going 0-3 in their first three games following the trade deadline?"

Why were the Mavs and other contenders so hopeful that the Clips would buy out Drew Gooden after facilitating the three-way deal that landed Jamison in Cleveland? Since landing in L.A., Gooden is averaging 16 and 10.

I'm guessing it'll surprise no one to learn that Tuesday's rout in Orlando coinciding with Mike Dunleavy's ouster was the Clips' league-worst sixth loss by 25 or more. Saturday's rout in San Antonio then made it seven.

Last week's most seismic upset? Forget Northern Iowa over Kansas. Try that Clips win over the scorching Bucks. It was L.A.'s only win in 10 games ... with the nine Ls coming by an unsightly average of 18 points.

Not to say that the Clips' win in Houston was unexpected, but they had dropped their previous 11 road games and Craig Smith -- who rumbled for 25 points and 10 boards -- had topped 20 points only once all season.

Our friends at Elias have unearthed a category that finds the Clips in the league lead. The problem? The category is games lost after leading by 20 points or more. Saturday's L in Denver was L.A.'s third such collapse.

Lone highlight of another Clipperesque season: Chris Kaman became the first player actually drafted by the Clips to represent them in the All-Star Game since 1988 draftee Danny Manning, who repped them in 1993.

mil.summary: Fun Bucks factoid to digest when you're not ripping yourself for underrating Brandon Jennings: Milwaukee has opened on the road for 25 seasons in a row! No one else in history has done so for more than 14 straight seasons.

Maybe the skeptics had it all wrong. Maybe the pairing of a brash, cocky young point guard (Jennings) with a very demanding coach who used to be a brash, cocky PG himself (Skiles) is actually a match that makes sense.

Who cares that three of the Bucks' wins came against teams with a combined record of 5-25? Milwaukee is suddenly synonymous with NBA excitement for the first time in forever. All because of one little lefty.

B-Jennings is the first rookie with six 25-points-or-more games before Thanksgiving since someone named Michael Jordan in November 1984. And you wonder why Scott Skiles can't get any pub for the job he's doing.

After all the slobbering over Jennings, we have to devote as much space to the little lefty's bad days, too. So here goes: Jennings has averaged just 14 points during the Bucks' four-game skid while shooting (gulp) 20-for-69.

Jennings busted out of his first pro freeze with 24 points in a home loss to Cleveland, but the chill lasted long enough -- 30 percent shooting during a 1-6 skid -- to hush any suggestion that the ROY race is already over.

Bogut's Twitter exclamation this weekend -- "11-11 baby!" -- got us thinking: Is it too soon to start wondering how many teams outside the top four in the East are going to wind up with a winning record?

Brandon Jennings' recent perimeter struggles don't worry the Bucks. Nor does the fact that 'Reke got the better of the rooks' first duel. The real crusher is that 1-8 record in games decided by three points or fewer.

Make that seven straight games under 20 points for young Jennings, who also decided not to retire from Twitter after all and just wrote this about his best game: "I believe that the 55 was a blessing and [a] curse."

Jennings knows how to get on the committee's good side. He heard Bucks fans lobbying via Twitter to break up my all-lefty backcourt by trading Redd for T-Mac's expiring deal. "THAT IS DUMB!" Jennings tweeted back.

I had literally just looked up from a mound of rankings research and switched the channel from Cavs-Blazers to Bucks-Lakers right when Michael Redd planted on that left knee ... and buckled. Evening ruined.

Although he was hoping to come back with a title contender, Stackhouse couldn't pass up this chance. Not with minutes available after Redd's injury and not with the Bucks still alive in the race for No. 8 in the East.

We can live with Brandon Jennings retiring his Twitter account. What we need is some drama in the ROY race. Jennings vs. Tyreke Evans, with no on-the-rise challengers, just ain't as epic as it seemed back in November.

A 3-10 record in games decided by three points or less is tough to take in any circumstance ... but it really leaves the East's No. 9 team with a sense of regret now that Toronto, Charlotte and Chicago have all gotten so hot.

He wears Throwball T-shirts to mock American football and just granted us a one-on-one. So I might be biased. But I do strongly believe Bogut is the best center I've seen in the East this season not named Dwight Howard.

Did Bogut deserve that East All-Star slot as Iverson's replacement as much as D-Lee? Hard to argue if winning is the thing, since the Bucks are 5.5 games closer to a playoff spot and given Bogut's impact at both ends.

Is it official? Can we safely declare that the race for playoff spots in the East has been whittled down to nine teams ... and that Skiles is right there with Larry Brown in the race for best coaching job in the conference?

No idea what took me so long to react. But the Bucks' overdue bump arrives now thanks to that 6-1 record since trading for Salmons and a 12-4 mark since Bogut's near-perfect game Jan. 26 in the committee's presence.

We still can't name him, but the advance scout who tabbed the Bucks as his surprise team of the season in the Weekend Dime isn't looking any less enlightened after the weekend. They're now 9-2 since the All-Star break.

We're going to tell you this anyway even though we're fairly sure you won't believe us: Milwaukee has the league's second-best record since the All-Star break at 12-2, just a half-game behind Dallas' 13-2 mark.

The Bulls surged in the second half last season after trading for John Salmons. The Bucks are 14-2 since trading for Salmons last month. Can't wait to see what kind of offers Milwaukee gets for the guy next February.

More (unlikely) props for the Bucks: They just suffered bad back-to-back home losses to Philly and Miami ... and yet people are still talking about how bad it'll be for Boston or Atlanta to face these guys in the first round.

It all comes crashing down for the second-half darlings in one brutal week: heartbreaking loss in Cleveland, OT loss in Charlotte and then the sickening loss of Bogut for the rest of the season to a gruesome elbow injury.

You can't, on one hand, give your ROY vote to a kid (even a lefty) shooting 37 percent from the field. But Jennings still has me second-guessing my pick, because you can't deny the effect he's had on a playoff team.

mem.summary: Considering they got drubbed at home in their opener by Detroit -- setting an unwanted NBA record with their ninth straight opening-night defeat -- all the offense we've seen since from the Grizz is pretty eye-catching.

No matter how cynical you are, surely you pegged the A.I.-Grizz marriage to make it at least past Thanksgiving. Didn't you? Throw in the 0-5 road trip and Memphis' story went from riveting to depressing in record time.

Full disclosure here: I want Iverson to come back soon purely and selfishly to see the Griz try to accommodate Rudy Gay, O.J. Mayo, Hasheem Thabeet, Marc Gasol, Zach Randolph, Iverson and now Jamaal Tinsley.

If we did Irony Rankings, Memphis would be a top-three lock. Grizz owner Michael Heisley mandated the signing of Iverson to be the first box-office draw in franchise history ... and A.I. left without playing a home game.

We were all set to wax poetic about how the one Iverson story no one is writing is how well Memphis has played since A.I. left. Then the Griz gave up 33 of the game's final 40 points to blow a 22-point lead in Clipperland.

Do you realize that the Grizz -- who now have three straight wins over Dallas after losing the previous 13 -- would be on an 8-3 roll if they had just finished off the Clips when they had 'em down by 22 in the fourth?

Yes: Zach Randolph should have been on the All-Star ballot. Yes: Rudy Gay has the whole league buzzing. Yes: Memphis is 4-1 in December and tempting us to use the R-word -- riveting -- even without Mr. Iverson.

Division leaders Cleveland, Dallas and now Denver are all Grizz victims, but I still can't seem to stop myself from wondering what we'd be saying if they had drafted a local collegian named Tyreke Evans over Thabeet.

As dangerous as the Grizz have been since their 1-8 start and the failed Iverson experiment, things could be even better. Saturday's loss in Dallas was their league-leading seventh in which they led by at least 10 points.

If I had said before the season that all but one team in the Southwest would be at .500 or better on the first Monday in January and that the Grizz would not be the sub-.500 team, what odds would you have given?

The Griz are back in the Southwest Division basement and awoke Monday as the West's No. 11 team, but read the fine print. They have to be right there with Houston and Sacramento at the top of the Cinderella Rankings.

The Grizz have clearly passed Sacramento, Houston and anyone else you want to suggest for the top of the Cinderella Rankings. Since Dec. 1, Memphis is 15-6 ... trailing only the Cavs (19-6) and Lakers (18-6).

The new leaders in the Cinderella Rankings are about to get their turn under the scrutiny lamp. Check out the opposition in four of Memphis' next six games: Magic and Lakers at home, then the Spurs and Cavs on the road.

Conversation that I never expected to have in January of the 2009-10 season: Prominent NBA player stops me in my tracks Saturday night to ask if I can believe that the Griz just lost at home to the CP3-less Hornets.

Saturday's trip to 'Sota figured to be a nice tonic after a stretch that wedged in stops in San Antonio and Cleveland with home dates against the Hornets, Lakers and Rockets. Except that the Wolves are suddenly no gimme, either.

Another hard-to-believe wrinkle in Memphis' improbable season: Who would have guessed, after a 10-3 start to 2010, that the Grizz would go 1-5 to start February … or that the one win would come against the Lakers?

The Grizzlies' rise to six games over .500 started to make you think that their 1-8 start would be what costs them a playoff berth ... only for a sudden 2-6 skid that they can't blame on Iverson hushing all such thoughts.

Four straight road wins account for just the latest in a string of Griz surprises, but here's the unfortunate reality out West: You've got to win 46 games to get to the playoffs if No. 8 Portland maintains its current pace.

The 1-8 start when they were still trying to get used to life with Iverson is one thing. Good luck explaining/rationalizing how the Grizz have managed to lose eight straight home games ... while winning six roadies in a row.

The Griz will own a slice of history no matter what happens from here. They're one of just two teams ever, along with Toronto in 2001-02, to win and lose at least eight straight games at home in the same season.

Even though they've been unquestionably better away from home since early February, I'm guessing that playing eight of their final 12 games on the road was not the Grizzlies' A scenario for making a late playoff push.

At 6½ games out of the final playoff spot in the West with nine to play, all the Griz can do now is try to secure a winning season by scraping out four more W's from a schedule offering just two more sub-.500 opponents.

It's not just the 1-8 start that cost the Griz their playoff ending to this Cinderella season. They've lost after leading by 10 or more 15 times, tops in the league ahead of 13 blown leads by Boston, Golden State, Houston.

After 55 double-doubles for Randolph and with a .500 record still within reach if the Griz can split their final two road games, in Denver and OKC, one question persists: Is Lionel Hollins still getting a contract extension?

ind.summary: Tyler Hansbrough's rookie debut is still on hold thanks to a shin problem. Mike Dunleavy's return from a long-term knee injury remains uncertain. And Team Granger is not nearly deep enough to cope well without them.

From the brink of its first 0-4 start since 1988-89, Indy's suddenly riding a modest win streak and reveling in the early success of Hibbert (11.0 ppg and 10.4 rpg) and Hansbrough (13 points in a 14-minute NBA debut).

We're with you, Pacer People. We watched your squad deliver another early season beatdown of the Celts -- just like last season -- and we're hoping this doesn't mean Indy is destined to peak in November. Again.

What drags a team back down to Earth after ringing up 113 points on Boston with Murphy, Dunleavy and Foster all out? The driving force in Indy's case was blowing a 13-point lead in the fourth quarter in New York.

Mike Dunleavy Jr. finally returned, but Hansbrough and Granger missed time with their own knee issues last week. Don't think you need reminding that Indy needs everybody to have any shot at the East's top eight.

The banged-up Pacers are in a 1-9 funk and just went 0-4 on a trip that included three of the West's more inviting stops, which sounds bad until you get to the worst part: Granger is going in for more tests on his heel.

Dunleavy's back at last, Hansbrough just had his first big NBA weekend and the finish against the Wiz couldn't have been more fortuitous. Not that the Pacers can celebrate after losing Granger for at least four weeks.

The ever-reliable Brian Windhorst reports that Troy Murphy is one of three PFs high on the Cavs' trade radar. We figured that Pacer People would rather ponder that than the team's recent Granger-less fortunes.

Another coach watch in the Central? Asked if his Granger-less team has quit after a 13-dunk humiliation from Miami, O'Brien told the Indy Star: "Certainly after getting beat this badly that's a very legitimate question."

The Pacers have actually weathered brief Granger absences in the past with near-.500 ball, but that was then. Now? Indy has lost nine of its last 10 games without its All-Star, including five double-digit poundings.

With Granger mercifully back from injury, T.J. Ford banished to the bench and the names of Jeff Foster and Troy Murphy coming up often in trade speculation, Indy is pretty newsy for a team stuck in the bottom five.

Granger's back, Troy Murphy is padding his trade value with every double-double and Indy just beat Toronto and Phoenix with comebacks from 23 and 24 points down, respectively. Best week of the season. By far.

There are four teams in the league, referring back to the Sixers' comment, that have blown nine double-digit leads this season: Philly, Houston, Memphis and Golden State. But Indy isn't far off the pace with seven.

Elias Sports Bureau to the comment rescue when Indy is playing its kids, shopping its vets and leaving us numb: Granger was held below double figures twice in January after going 56-for-56 in the 2009 calendar year.

Conseco remains one of the best basketball temples you could ever wish to visit. But not even yours truly would dare claim that these Pacers or even their top-shelf building can lift the locals out of their Colts-induced gloom.

The Pacers have placed ninth in the East for three straight seasons … which must sound heavenly compared to their current plight: No. 13 in the East and no All-Star rep. Unless you count TNT's Reggie Miller.

Two unexpected developments: T.J. Ford has returned from exile with two 20-point games already .. and Indy nearly found a taker for Ford on trade-deadline day before its deal for Charlotte's D.J. Augustin collapsed.

Saw Larry Bird on NBA TV over the weekend discussing A) Indy's long and difficult "journey" until it has cap space in the summer of 2011 and B) how he expected this group to at least make another run at 35-40 wins.

Any Pacer People out there remember that 5-3 start? Or shall we rephrase the question: Any Pacer People out there prepared to raise your hands? Tough times unless you happen to be watching the new Reggie Miller doc.

The Pacers' season peaked at approximately 9 p.m. Sunday. That's when -- hours after Indy extended its road losing streak to eight with an L in Milwaukee -- ESPN rolled out the new Reggie Miller documentary.

Enough is enough? Apparently fed up after Dunleavy was KO'd when a ball hit him in the eye during layup lines, Indy uncorked a 3-1 week, beating playoff-bound Charlotte and OKC and taking its home win streak to four.

Just keepin' it real: Indy's five-game win streak that ended in Atlanta and seven consecutive wins at home don't change the fact that you still think docs (Reggie Miller or Larry/Magic) when you think Pacers these days.

The good news: This 7-2 run with nothing to play for has to hush some of those rumbles about players bailing on Jim O'Brien. The bad news: This 7-2 run with nothing to play for ain't exactly improving Indy's lottery odds.

We leave it to you, Pacer People: Encouraged by this late-season surge? Or enraged by a 10-2 finish that has Indy -- needing as much help in the draft as it can find -- headed for just the league's 10th-worst record?

min.summary: The comeback win over Jersey was nice, but nothing at this stage matters more than the recovery of Al Jefferson, who looked a little more like himself in Phoenix with 21 points ... after totaling 21 in the first two games.

New coach. Familiar start. Minnesota won a two-point game on opening night last season, then dropped the next eight. Kurt Rambis needs a win Monday at Golden State or Wednesday vs. Portland to avoid the same.

This is only the fifth time ever three teams started 1-9 (or worse) in the same season. The Wolves weren't supposed to be in Knicks/Nets territory, but you can't be surprised looking at their team minus Love and Jefferson.

It must be worrisome for the Wolves, to say the least, that they've played almost into Thanksgiving and somehow Ricky Rubio has tasted victory in the NBA only one fewer time than fellow Wolves lottery pick Jonny Flynn.

This was only the second time two teams have started 1-15 or worse in the same season. Which is why there isn't a soul who can get away with claiming that he/she saw the Wolves winning in Denver to get to 2-15.

Kevin Love returned from a broken hand with a flourish, but that was just the second-best thing to happen to the Wolves last week. No. 1: They're suddenly on pace for a record-avoiding 12 wins after a win over Utah.

Even after that recent stunner in Denver, Minnesota can't avoid slipping into the cellar. Not when the Wolves have six losses this season by at least 20 points … or three times as many as New Jersey in that category.

We'd like to think that demoting the Wolves to No. 30 was the inspiration for that stunning win at Utah. We'd also like to explain how the Wolves now have huge divisional road wins at Denver and Utah. But we can't.

Two wins over Utah, Kevin Love's nightly double-doubles and the gradual awakening of Corey Brewer have almost enabled long-suffering Wolves fans to focus their displeasure purely on the winter weather. Almost.
That was even more unpleasant than usual. The Wolves just missed out on a third upset of Utah when they couldn't finish off a late comeback from 17 down, then got pushed around in Indy.

Maybe Jefferson and Love can't work long term as a tag team because neither provides shot-blocking or defensive athleticism. But breaking them up now, after basically a half-season under Rambis, is risky. Thoughts?

The bad news: 'Sota has zero games left against the Nets. The good news: New Jersey continues to hog the futility spotlight even with the Wolves on a 16-66 pace and sporting a 9.9-point average margin of defeat.

It's a tough sell even for us to pitch the Wolves as an outfit capable of lifting spirits in devastated 'Sota when the local hoopsters have played 45 games ... and still need four wins just to match the Vikes' season total.

The Wolves don't play again until Friday, which either rubs out their first bit of momentum for ages or gives them almost a week to savor just their second win streak of the season. (We agree: It's probably the latter.)

Whether it's Brewer's under-the-radar progress, K-Love's acceptance of a sixth-man role or the improving grasp of the triangle offense, interesting things are happening in 'Sota. Worth a look in spite of the record.

Maybe it's not the most pressing issue confronting the Wolves these days, but just throwing it out there again: Don't you have to bring up Kurt Rambis when the whole Shaq-versus-Dwight Superman debate comes up?

The Wolves' recent four-game win streak is a memory, replaced by a six-game skid. Love's 10 double-doubles off the bench -- second in the league to Miami's Udonis Haslem -- is the most upbeat tidbit we could find.

The Blazers must have been paying attention when 'Sota sneaked in those road wins in Utah and Denver, because they just polished off a very focused four-game sweep of the Wolves. Margins: 23, 23, 24 and 19.

Hard to see our man K-Love making a real push in the Sixth Man Award race with the Wolves getting thumped anew, but it is worth noting he's tops in the league in double-doubles off the bench with a solid 14.

The Wolves have twice as many wins as New Jersey, but they're also 1-15 since that four-game win streak before the All-Star break. Which makes them the easiest out in the league these days ... essentially tied for No. 30.

The nicest thing you can say about the Wolves during this ghastly 1-18 spell is that they probably couldn't drop into the No. 30 cellar even if they wanted to ... unless the Nets can win two games in a row for the first time all season.

We warned the Wolves what would happen if the Nets ever managed two wins in the same week. The fact that Sota is the first team since the '97-98 Nuggets with two 15-game skids in the same season left us no choice.

Sota is stuck down in the No. 30 basement for a second successive week -- with only one more Monday to get out -- even though its record isn't worse than New Jersey's. That's pretty much the worst of both worlds.

The Wolves have dropped 21 of 22 and are openly acknowledging that Love and Jefferson both play better next to Darko than they do alongside each other. Not expecting much protest, then, to their placement in the cellar.

gsw.summary: As if the Dubs don't have enough going on, they're still smarting from the one-point home L to Houston. Good thing their next four games (Grizz, Clips, Wolves at home and Sac-Town away) offer four chances to atone.

The first six games on the Dubs' schedule were super-favorable. And you've seen the results. So you'd be quite brave to suggest that Golden State is going to find harmony on its five-game swing through the East.

Isn't the Jack trade alone worthy of this bump? This we believe even more firmly: Nellie is not going to walk away from his $6 million salary to drop to a consultant's wage, nor will the Dubs pay him $6 mil just to consult.

The Dubs can't relax now that Jack's gone. Not when a W over Portland was preceded by L's at Cleveland and Boston. And not when stops in Dallas and San Antonio are next before a home date with the Lakers.

A run of six straight games against top-flight teams ended with a 33-point hammering from the Lakers. The Dubs would prefer that we focus on the wins over Portland and Dallas, but that depends on what happens next.

The Warriors have allowed 120 points or more an NBA-worst six times. So you could do a lot worse than seeing your team hook up with Golden State if that's the only shot you get all season to see a game in person.

What do Monta Ellis, Michael Finley and Latrell Sprewell have in common? They're the only three players in the past 35 years to play all 48 minutes at least five times before Christmas ... with Nellie coaching in each case.

This is the month teams down here started consoling themselves with the same two-word draft prayer: John Wall. Even teams like the Warriors, who are awash in guards with Monta and Steph Curry and need a big.

Love this stat so I'm re-using it after Weekend Dime usage: Monta has played all 48 minutes six times this season ... after 20 of 30 MLB teams got fewer than six complete games from their starting staffs last season.

Although the Dubs couldn't build on huge back-to-back wins over Phoenix and Boston, they're finally putting proven NBA size on the floor thanks to the returns of Biedrins and Turiaf. And Monta does need the help.

The Monta Ellis Show has been in Oaktown for a league-low 14 home games. So maybe Don Nelson isn't as far from the record for all-time coaching wins -- currently 12 shy of Lenny Wilkens' 1,332 -- as it seems.
I've heard/read more All-Star pub for Monta Ellis in his big-numbers-on-a-

If West coaches pass because of the Dubs' record, Monta will become just the second player ever averaging at least 25 points, five assists and two steals to be an ASG snub, joining Denver's Michael Adams in 1990-91.

Even when there's some upbeat news, there's a caveat: Steph Curry looks like he's making a surge into the ROY race ... but that's bound to get folks whispering anew about the Dubs moving Monta for Curry's benefit.

If Monta Ellis is not selected as B-Roy's injury replacement for Sunday's All-Star Game at Cowboys Stadium, there is a consolation prize: Another crack Monday night at the Dallas defense Monta just shredded for 46 points.
Don Nelson emerged from the All-Star break needing 11 wins to pass Lenny Wilkens for the all-time lead in coaching victories. When you scan the Dubs' remaining schedule, do you see 11 winnable games?

Curry is clearly making a ROY charge after averaging 20.4 ppg and 7.3 apg in February, but the Dubs had better have a big summer planned to atone for the trade they just turned down: Monta for Mayo and Thabeet.

You tell me: Which stretch-run milestone happens first? New Jersey gets to 10 wins? Or the Dubs win the seven games that nudge Nellie (1,326) past Lenny Wilkens (1,332) as the all-time winningest coach in league history?

Interesting wrinkle in what looks like a two-rook ROY race between the Dubs' Steph Curry and the Kings' Tyreke Evans: Records don't really factor in when the two teams are on pace for 23 and 27 wins, respectively.

I suspect it isn't branching out onto the most dangerous limb to suggest that Steph Curry trying to chase down Tyreke Evans in the ROY race holds Oaktown's interest more than Don Nelson versus Lenny Wilkens.

The Warriors have lost 13 consecutive road games, allowing at least 99 points in every single one of them. The significance? Elias Sports Bureau says no team has been that easy on the road since Milwaukee in '93-94.

The sale of the team won't get hot until the firm that's heading the sale collects all the Dubs' financial data, so the focus is all on Curry (in the ROY race) and Nellie (suddenly just three W's from the wins record) for now.

More evidence that the Curry-Monta backcourt will eventually be broken up? The Dubs sure don't play worse when Monta's out, improving to a decent 6-9 when Ellis sits this season with Nellie's record-tying W in Toronto.

The Dubs got Nellie his record with a surprising 7-7 spurt and stayed on course to post the league's third-worst record. It was shaping up to be the best ending they could have hoped for until they went and stunned OKC.

nyk.summary: Knicks fans have suffered so much for so long that we've made the benevolent decision to focus on a glimmer of positivity -- Gallinari's electric start -- as opposed to everything excruciating we've already seen.

You'd have struggled this weekend to hear anyone use decent or fight in a sentence about the Knicks. Friday against Cleveland and Saturday in Milwaukee, New York surrendered 40 points in the first quarter.

In the midst of four full days off after a humbling home loss to Golden State, we can come up with only one thing going right for the Knicks: Dare we say they're not the only team that missed on Brandon Jennings.

This is where they draw the line? After a decade of stupefying Knicks madness and dysfunction, Iverson is the guy they won't sign? Would have actually made the rest of the Knicks' season fun. Or at least watchable.

The good news: Al Harrington has somehow erupted for 40 points or more twice off the bench. The bad news: Harrington's Knicks have surrendered four of the league's past 10 50-point games after Melo's 50 on Friday.

Maybe it's a tad early to start throwing around the V word -- vindication -- but the Knicks have been hard to second-guess since electing not to finalize their intended signing of A.I. As Phoenix or Atlanta could tell you.

It's still too early for the V-word -- vindication -- but going 5-1 in December with wins over three legit teams (Phoenix, Atlanta and Portland) is the best Knicks stretch we can remember in, um, a really long time.

We've all been so wrapped up in the Nate Robinson drama that we almost missed Mike D'Antoni's Knicks -- we repeat: Mike D'Antoni's Knicks -- holding seven straight foes below 100 points in their 7-3 December.

You'll recall that Isiah got a contract extension in 2007 for getting the Knicks up to No. 8 in the East for a sec. With a top-eight slot and a 10-win December still in reach for these Knicks, what should D'Antoni expect?

Add up David Lee's still-underrated board work, Nate Rob's fairy-tale return from exile and New York's 10-5 spell of decency and suddenly the s-l-o-w countdown to July 1 is bearable, 'cause the team is watchable.

Grizzlies of the East? Sounds like a slam, but it's not. The Knicks, you see, endured an even worse start than Memphis -- 1-9 compared with 1-8 -- but have rebounded with the East's third-best record (12-7) since Dec. 1.

How freaked must the Knicks be about Friday's date with the Lakers? Kobe scored 61 points in his previous MSG appearance ... and Friday happens to be the fourth anniversary of his 81-point detonation against Toronto.

Hard to believe the Knicks -- 14-10 since that 4-13 start -- entered the weekend as the NBA's most improved team since Dec. 1. Really, really hard to believe after Dallas trounced them in their orange socks by 50.

Maybe the coaches who snubbed David Lee knew what was coming. Losing both ends of a back-to-back in Washington and Sota since the ASG snub makes it way harder to claim that Lee's Knicks are in the East playoff mix.

The Knicks started 3-14, won 12 of the next 18 and then tumbled again with losses in 11 of the past 15. Add it all up and you inevitably conclude that D-Lee is going to struggle for an All-Star spot even as an injury replacement.

Don't get me wrong. I'm a D-Lee fan and happy to confirm that the lefty point forward is only the second Knicks draftee post-Ewing to represent any team in the All-Star Game, joining my beloved Mark Jackson.

Where does 26 points in 32 minutes rank on the list of T-Mac debuts? It has to be No. 1 based on expectations and isn't far off from No. 1 production-wise. Houston debut: 18 points. Orlando debut: 32. Toronto debut: 0.

It hasn't stopped the sniping about his David Stern-issued All-Star invite, thanks to all the Knicks' recent losing, but D-Lee just averaged 23.5 ppg in February, good for the third straight "best" scoring month of his career.

That groan you just heard came from New Yorkers who don't want to read or hear a word about how tough the No. 6 Jazz have it. Every ugly loss that the Knicks pile up only sweetens that first-round pick bound for Utah.

Would love to explain how these Knicks could lose to the Mavs by 50 at MSG, then orchestrate an 84-point turnaround in Dallas. But we weren't in our usual courtside seat, so we're still not sure this actually happened.

D'Antoni takes a lot of heat for a coach whose team's primary objective for the past two seasons has been clearing salary-cap space. His critics really expected him to take the Knicks to the playoffs at the same time?

Best-case scenario at this stage? Probably finishing with the league's 10th-worst record -- about as high as the Knicks can go at this point -- and hope nothing crazy happens in the lottery so the pick sent to Utah is 10th overall.

Our Elias data isn't any more upbeat for the Knicks than it is for the Clips. Elias says N.Y. will be the league's only team with an active streak of at least five straight losing seasons as soon as Charlotte wins twice more.

Twitter pal Noam Schiller sums up the challenges of New York's l-o-n-g wait for 2010 free agency: "Raise your hand if, two years ago, you predicted that T-Mac, Earl Barron and an Italian dude would start for the Knicks."

bkn.summary: The Nets are painfully thin and young (and counting down the days to 2010 free agency) even when Devin Harris is healthy. So we might as well keep talking about the incoming Russian billionaire if Harris is out injured.

Even though we're already wondering, just like you, if the Nets are really at risk to challenge the 0-17 record for Worst Start Ever, they avoid our cellar because they're putting up a decent fight with eight healthy bodies.

Indy at home Tuesday night. Milwaukee on the road Wednesday night. And a big Saturday lunchtime showdown with the equally punchless Knicks. Surely winless New Jersey can win one of three games this week. Right?

L-Frank won his first 13 games as an NBA head coach after replacing Byron Scott. And now Frank's in the midst of an 0-13 start in what is virtually certain to be his final season in New Jersey. Did someone say full circle?

Can't tell you quite yet who the next coach will be. Can tell you that three of the Nets' next five games (Friday vs. Charlotte, Saturday at New York and Dec. 9 vs. Golden State) would appear to be (somewhat) winnable.

Kiki Vandeweghe on the congratulatory messages he received after winning his first game to become the first coach in NBA history to halt an 18-game losing streak: "Most of them said you should retire right now."

Just ruminating out loud: If the Nets could add John Wall in the draft to Devin Harris, Brook Lopez, Jay-Z as minority owner and an eventual move to Brooklyn … would they have a legitimate shot at landing LeBron then?

More unwanted milestones: New Jersey is just the seventh team in history to rack up 25 losses in 27 games after Friday's defeat in Toronto. The last to do so was New Orleans, which also started 2-25 in 2004-05.

The guess here is that it won't surprise you to hear that the Nets just tied five predecessors (most recently New Orleans in 2004-05) for the worst 30-game start in NBA history. Which means they're on a (yikes) 5-77 pace.

It took a seven-game homestand and help from the snoozing Knicks, but the Nets finally found the win that kept them away from the record for most losses before a team's third W. Dallas went 2-39 in 1993-94.

Can't be easy to lock in when your team is 0-15 against the West, stuck on a 7-75 pace and stuck waiting for the official arrival of a new owner and summer cap space. But Devin Harris could be doing more. Couldn't he?

The Nets' record through 39 games equals the 3-36 mark posted by Philadelphia through 39 games in its fateful 9-73 season in 1972-73. The Sixers' fourth victory, in case you're wondering, came in game No. 42.

Chilling stat of the day: Take away those two wins in Kiki's first three games as coach and the Nets, folks, are 1-39. They're also getting worse somehow: 0-11 in January with an average losing margin of 19.6 ppg.

The post-victory celebration after win No. 4 didn't last long. Home losses to the Wiz and Sixers by a combined six points, in what looks like the Nets' most favorable stretch of schedule remaining, will have that effect.

OK, OK. The Nets surely need the All-Star break even more than the Celts, given that they just tied the 1972-73 Sixers and 1992-93 Mavs for the worst 50-game start in league history and since they're on pace to finish 7-75.

The Nets want Jerry Colangelo, Coach K and John Wall before they even get to free agency? At least the team that still needs to muster five wins in its final 29 games to steer clear of NBA infamy hasn't lost its ambition.

The bad news: New Jersey is still on a 7-75 pace even after emerging from the All-Star break with a thoroughly unexpected win in Charlotte. The worse news: New Jersey is 2-1 against the Bobs but plays them only once more.

The shocker heard 'round the world in Boston just catapulted the Nets two wins ahead of Philly's fateful 9-73 pace through 58 games in 1972-73. Which means you can almost hear the exhales from here. Almost.

Extending Memphis' home losing skid to nine would give the Nets their first back-to-back wins of the season. Which would also somehow give them four straight Ws on the road. Which is why our tone is so skeptical.

The Nets are close enough that you figure they're going to get the three wins they need to dodge infamy. But with a 1-7 mark in games decided by three points or fewer, they'll have plenty to second-guess if they don't.

The committee (of one) doesn't want to be so alarmist, but even the 1972-73 Sixers had nine wins by this stage. Philly didn't win another game that season, true, but 9-60 has to sound pretty good to the Nets right now.

The Nets still need one more W in their final nine games for a full exhale, but they have made sure that they won't become the fourth team in history to go through an entire season without winning two straight games.

These are the kinds of fun hypotheticals we get to throw around about the Nets now that they've passed the nine-win mark: What if Prokhorov just decides to keep raising his offer until he gets a "yes" from Coach K?

They'd love to celebrate avoiding the all-time worst record, finishing the season higher than 30th and leaving the Meadowlands for good ... but so much as breathing is on hold until Prokhorov is approved as the new owner.

sac.summary: As much as we'd like to dissect/dwell on Casspi's debut, we can't ignore the reality that any and all rookie discussion in Sacramento will focus on Tyreke Evans' recovery from a twisted ankle. Until Evans is back.

Never thought the Kings would move out of the No. 30 basement this quickly. Also never imagined they could follow up a home win over Memphis with Nocioni's arrest and Kevin Martin's injury ? and then win in Utah.

Fitting that Houston was the victim when the Kings extended their miraculous, shocker-of-the-season start to 5-4. Sacramento's scrappy play without the injured Kevin Martin does feel rather Rockets-esque.

No Kevin Martin or Tyreke Evans in Houston and still Sacramento hangs in all the way to the final minute on the back end of a back-to-back. One more example of why we refer this scrappy group of kids as Rockets Lite.

The Kings take a .500 record into December. We repeat: Sacramento is a .500 team despite losing Kev Martin to a wrist injury. With apologies to anyone else worth nominating, this is your Surprise Team of November.

Can't quibble with the 14-3 record posted by Alvin Gentry in November, so long as we don't forget Westy's 8-8 mark with the upstart Kings. Surely just as worthy of the first Western Conference coach of the month award.

Ten wins already and nine at home for Sacramento's young overachievers. The Kings didn't get win No. 10 in 2008-09 until Jan. 14 and won only 11 games all season at what was an Arco fortress in the glory days.

One of my best Hanukkah presents: Casspi has been so good that it's totally natural to talk about him all the time. Tyreke has been a certifiable stud … but my guy's coming to Dallas for the Rookie Game, too.

Way too soon to think about trading Kevin Martin. Not until the Kings get a longer look at how he plays next to Tyreke ... and not after Ls in OT to the Cavs and Lakers that cried out for an experienced scorer in crunch time.

You can dwell on how poorly they handled the final play when Kobe got the most wide-open buzzer 3 he'll ever see. Or you can focus on how the Kings, without Tyreke, beat Denver and lost to the Lakers by a point.

We should probably focus on the recent five-game skid as opposed to our guy Casspi's run of four straight 20-point games. Or we could just tell you Kevin Martin should be back soon to make the Kings really interesting.

Remember when we said that Kevin Martin would be back soon to make things really interesting for the early pace setters in the Cinderella Rankings? Perhaps we should have gone with the word complicated.

The 13-14 start was hard to fathom, but the subsequent 2-14 nosedive is almost as hard to process. And don't even get me started on what the losing and struggles to reintegrate Kevin Martin have done to our beloved Casspi.

The way things have unraveled -- 3-16 since a 13-14 start -- it looks like it'll be a l-o-n-g string for the Kings to play out after the highlight of the season: Tyreke and our man Casspi teaming up in Dallas for the Rookie Game.

Everyone loves the Kings' draft, but GM Geoff Petrie's best move might have been securing his contract extension when he did. The Kings had just beaten Denver at home to improve to 14-16. They're 2-18 since.

Upset of the season: Omri Casspi was all over the place in Dallas … and the closest that the committee (of one) got to him during a whirlwind All-Star Weekend was a baseline seat for Friday's Rookie Game.

The immediate impact of the Carl Landry trade? Sacramento just shook up the Sixth Man Award race by dealing for Landry to anchor its frontcourt, eliminating Jamal Crawford's foremost threat in the sixth-man race.

We certainly didn't expect Westphal's Kings to need this long to reach 20 wins after a 13-14 start ... but we can also still remember plenty of folks back in October who thought this team's ceiling was less than 20 wins.

Our beloved Casspi was back in Dallas on Friday night for the last time as a rookie, while the committee [of one] was on a plane bound for Dorkapalooza. Which is the only bad thing we can say about the weekend.

Tyreke is still averaging 20, 5 and 5, something only Oscar Robertson, Michael Jordan and LeBron James did as rooks. Which is why Tyreke is still the ROY favorite ahead of his fast-charging Golden State neighbor.

Even if you think he's already done enough to clinch the ROY trophy you're obviously hoping Evans is back soon to finish his rookie season strong. Casspi can't make the Kings watchable on his own ... except maybe for us.

Udrih is averaging 18.2 ppg and 11.8 apg in the five games Tyreke Evans has missed since suffering a concussion. Not sure how much more of the Reke-less Kings we can take, though. (Especially with Casspi's PT down.)

I'm afraid that the ROY race will be closer than you think for Reke. Blame Curry's second-half numbers and his popularity/stature and Jennings' quality contributions to a playoff-bound team despite his statistical decline.

Remember when we asked whether we'd see more Kings wins or Casspi mentions in 24 weeks of regular-season rankings? Even I'm surprised it wasn't closer: 25 W's for Tyreke's Kings ... and nine Omri references.
